summary: Loop-Free Alternates are an IP Fast Reroute mechanism that protects traffic. Based on early deployment, this standards-track RFC provides operational feedback, highlights limitations, proposes refinements and defines required management specifications.

eli5.summary: Lessons from using backup routes in real networks, with fixes and ways to manage them.

questions: how to choose the best lfa
subtitle: Field lessons on Loop-Free Alternates, plus the policy, monitoring and troubleshooting features operators need to manage them.

tldr.problem: Loop-Free Alternates give routers a precomputed backup path, but the default way of picking among several candidates can choose badly, for example sending core traffic over thin edge links, and operators lack ways to control or observe the choice.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes four real-world problem cases and then sets requirements for per-scope activation, a policy framework with ranked criteria (protection type, shortest path, SRLGs, link and node coloring, bandwidth), and visibility, alerting and testing features.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get a common list of manageability features to build, and they apply to remote-LFA too. The RFC adds no new security considerations over RFC 5286.

today: RFC 7916 is a Proposed Standard from July 2016 and, per the registry metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 5286 and also applies to remote-LFA solutions as described in RFC 7490.

sections.title: Why LFAs Need Managing
sections.content:
Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs), defined in RFC 5286, are an IP Fast Reroute mechanism. A router precomputes a backup next hop so that traffic can switch to it quickly when a link or node fails. This RFC reports on early deployments, highlights limitations, proposes refinements and sets management requirements. It also applies to remote-LFA solutions.

The RFC defines a few terms. The Point of Local Repair (PLR) is the router that reroutes. A connected alternate is an IGP neighbor of the PLR, while a remote alternate shares no IGP adjacency with it. A link-protecting LFA covers link failure and a node-protecting LFA covers node failure. The analysis assumes per-prefix computation, where the best alternate is chosen for each destination prefix.
sections.eli5: A backup route is like a spare detour. This document is about how real network operators found that the default detours are not always the smart ones, and how to manage them.

sections.title: Four Problems with Default Tiebreakers
sections.content:
RFC 5286 picks among several candidate LFAs mainly by how much failure coverage they offer. The RFC says this is one goal among several, and in some deployments it leads to a suboptimal choice. It walks through four cases.

  • Case 1: when a core link fails, the only available LFA is a PE router. PE links usually have less capacity than core links, so they may congest, and traffic not affected by the failure may suffer too.
  • Case 2: a P router offers a link-protecting LFA and a PE router offers a node-protecting one. The PE router wins because of the better protection type, with the same congestion risk.
  • Case 3: a node-protecting alternate is chosen, but it sits on a lower-bandwidth link. Preferring the shortest path would only help if metrics reflect bandwidth.
  • Case 4: a node with the no-transit condition set (IS-IS overload bit, OSPF R-bit, or OSPF stub router) cannot use a neighbor that would never loop traffic back to it, because the loop-free inequality fails. LFA behavior in that case needs to be clarified.
sections.eli5: The default rule picks the detour that covers the most trouble, even if it is a narrow lane that jams up. Sometimes a wider road is the better choice.

sections.title: Coverage Monitoring and Activation Granularity
sections.content:
LFA coverage depends strongly on topology, as RFC 6571 notes, and topologies keep changing. Even remote-LFA (RFC 7490) leaves some cases unprotected. A provider must always know what protection is available now and should be able to predict it after a topology change. The RFC asks for LFA information in planning tools and in routers, so operators can evaluate coverage after a change, adjust changes to keep protection, and monitor the live network with alerts. Vendors are asked to document their selection algorithms so third-party tools can model them.

Backup paths use Forwarding Information Base (FIB) resources, and generally only a few destinations, such as loopback addresses supporting MPLS services, need protection. Turning LFA on everywhere by default may waste FIB space. An implementation MAY also compute alternates for a destination already protected by another FRR mechanism, such as MRT or TE FRR, and let a policy language choose.
sections.eli5: Backup plans use up space in a router's memory, so protect the important places rather than everything. And keep checking that your backup roads still work after the map changes.

sections.title: Configuration Requirements
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD let operators control activation per routing context (VRF, logical router, global table), per interface, and per protocol instance, topology or area. They SHOULD also allow per-prefix activation, which has higher priority than interface protection: if a prefix is configured for protection, an LFA MUST be computed for it even if its primary outgoing interface is not. Per address family and per MPLS control plane (inheriting protection from IP prefixes to labels) are MAY options.

Selection should be policy based. The policy SHOULD use multiple criteria, each with a level of preference. If it cannot find one unique best LFA, the implementation picks one itself, and it SHOULD also support electing several for load balancing. A policy can apply to a protected interface or to a set of destinations. Whether policy changes are re-evaluated dynamically is up to the implementation. If not dynamic, a command to force recomputation SHOULD exist.

The selection MUST consider all available alternates, connected or tunnel. Tunnels (IP, GRE, LDP, RSVP-TE, L2TP, Segment Routing and others) can reach remote alternates, and with remote LFAs the PQ sets SHOULD be computed before selection.
sections.eli5: Operators need switches to say where backup routes are turned on, and a rule book to rank the detours, so the best detour wins every time.

sections.title: Policy Criteria and Path Attributes
sections.content:
An implementation MUST support these criteria: a non-candidate link marker (never used as an LFA), protection of one ECMP primary next hop by another, protection type (link or node, with fallback to link protection when node protection is not available), shortest path (lowest IGP metric), and Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs). It SHOULD support preference for downstream alternates, link coloring, link bandwidth, and alternate preference or node coloring.

  • SRLGs: alternates in violation can be excluded or ranked by number of violations or by violation cost. The check covers source-to-alternate and alternate-to-destination parts.
  • Link coloring: links carry colors, and a protected interface includes some colors with a preference and excludes others. Colors SHOULD be signaled with existing administrative-group extensions. In the RFC's example, PE links are RED and excluded, the 10 Gbps core link is BLUE with preference 200, and the 1 Gbps core link is YELLOW with preference 100.
  • Bandwidth: based on link speed, since a router does not know the traffic volume it must protect. It can prune an LFA whose link is slower than the primary, or prefer by relative speed.
  • Node coloring: routers carry tags advertised in the IGP (see RFC 7917 and RFC 7777), so groups of alternates can be preferred or excluded.

Each alternate path has two parts: PLR to alternate, and alternate to destination. Criteria need attributes of the path, such as SRLG, bandwidth, color or tag. A cumulative attribute (SRLG, link color, node color) is recorded on every element along the path. A unitary attribute (bandwidth) is recorded only on the first element.

For a connected alternate, the first part comes from the interface to the alternate. If several interfaces reach it, each is evaluated as a separate alternate, but an ECMP group (Layer 3 bundle) is evaluated once. The second part comes from the shortest path tree rooted at the alternate, which was already computed. For a remote alternate, the first part comes from the PLR's primary tree or the neighbor's tree, and the second part may need an extra forward tree for each PQ node.

Remote LFAs can have hundreds of PQs in real topologies, so implementations need to limit how many they evaluate before collecting attributes. When a path fans out over ECMP, the union of the attributes of the sub-paths is used.
sections.eli5:
The rule book lets you say things like: never use the small side streets, prefer the widest road, and avoid detours that share a bridge with the closed road.

To judge a detour you look at every road along it. Some facts, like road color, are noted for every piece. Others, like the speed limit, only for the first piece.

sections.title: ECMP, Manual Triggering and No-Transit Nodes
sections.content:
When a primary path uses ECMP, standard behavior after a failure leaves only the surviving next hop. If the parallel links are configured as a Layer 3 bundle, an implementation SHOULD instead be able to use another bundle as the LFA to keep bandwidth. Implementations SHOULD allow preferring another primary next hop, or a non-primary one, as the alternate, and SHOULD allow an ECMP bundle as an LFA.

For the no-transit condition, besides the loop-free inequality the LFA computing node's own IS-IS overload bit or OSPF R-bit SHOULD be taken into account: if the overload bit is set or the R-bit is clear, no neighbor will loop traffic back to it. An OSPF stub router (RFC 6987) SHOULD behave as if the R-bit were clear.

Testing FRR needs ways to trigger it. An implementation SHOULD trigger LFA FRR when a manual shutdown is done on a component that normally triggers it, such as a BFD session or a physical interface. It MAY allow FRR activation for one interface or prefix without touching any running component, under a timer that reverts traffic automatically if the operator forgets.
sections.eli5: Operators need a safe way to pretend a road is closed and watch the detour work, with an alarm clock that puts everything back afterwards.

sections.title: Visibility, Alerts and Planning
sections.content:
An implementation MUST display, for every prefix, the primary and alternate next hops. It MUST provide coverage information per LFA activation domain and the number of protected and non-protected prefixes globally. It SHOULD provide those counts per link, SHOULD explain why an alternate was chosen or excluded, and SHOULD list unprotected prefixes with the reason (for example, no alternate available).

It SHOULD alert when total coverage for a node, or coverage for a specific link, falls below a threshold or returns to normal, and MAY alert for a specific destination. Mechanisms are out of scope, but the RFC suggests syslog or SNMP traps.

For network planning, an implementation SHOULD behave deterministically: with the same topology and policy it MUST always choose the same alternate for a prefix. It SHOULD also document its behavior well enough that a simulation tool can predict the exact choice, for example by disclosing its algorithm.
sections.eli5: A router should be able to tell you what its backup plan is, shout if the plan gets worse, and always pick the same backup in the same situation so planners can predict it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The policy mechanism only tunes which alternate is selected. The RFC does not see this as a security threat, because all candidates are already eligible under RFC 5286 and considered usable, and the policy relies on the router's own configuration and on IGP information, both considered trusted. It therefore adds no new security considerations compared to RFC 5286, which notes that the best alternate can be used anyway when a different topological change occurs.
sections.eli5: The new rules only change which already-allowed detour is chosen, so they do not open new doors for attackers.

viz.caption: CRITERIA, AS REQUIRED OR RECOMMENDED BY THE RFC

items.label: Non-candidate link
items.desc: A link marked non-candidate is never used as an LFA.

items.label: Protection type
items.desc: Link or node protection, with fallback to link protection.

items.label: Shortest path
items.desc: Lowest IGP metric to the destination.

items.label: SRLGs
items.desc: Exclude or rank alternates that share risk with the primary.

items.label: Downstream preference
items.desc: Prefer a downstream path over a non-downstream one.

items.label: Link coloring
items.desc: Include, exclude and rank by link color.

items.label: Link bandwidth
items.desc: Prune or prefer by link speed.

items.label: Node coloring
items.desc: Prefer or exclude alternates by IGP tag.
